chunks: And by this chain, I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying:

He was asked about enjoining the good and forbidding the evil: 'Is it obligatory upon the entire community?' He said: 'No.' It was said to him: 'And why?' He said: 'Rather, it is upon the strong, the obeyed, who is knowledgeable of the good and the evil, not upon the weak who is not guided of the way, to which from which, he should be speaking from the truth to the falsehood.'
And from among you there should be a community inviting to the better and enjoin what is good and forbid the evil.

Thus, these are particular ones and not the general public, just as Allah Mighty and Majestic Said: 'And of Musa's people was a party who guided (people) with the truth, and thereby did they do justice.' And He did not Say: 'And it is upon the people of Musa', nor 'Upon every one of his people', and in those days they were different communities, and the community can be one (man), just as Allah Mighty and Majestic Said that: 'Surely Ibrahim was a community, obedient to Allah'.

He is Saying: 'Obedient to Allah Mighty and Majestic'. And it is not upon the one who knows that in these times of truce from danger, when there was not strength for him, nor an excuse, and do obedience.

Mas'ada said, 'And I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying, and he was asked about the Hadeeth which came from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) that: 'The most superior of the Jihad is the just word in the presence of an unjust leader', what is its meaning?' He said: 'This is upon a stipulation that he would enjoin him (with the good) after having recognised it (himself), and along with that, he (the leader) would accept it from him, or else, so no!'.
ai.seo_question: Is enjoining the good and forbidding the evil obligatory on every Muslim or only on specific individuals?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the individual obligation (fard al-ayn) and the communal obligation (fard al-kifaya) of enjoining good, specifying that the latter applies to the knowledgeable and influential who can effectively implement it. He supports this by interpreting the Quranic phrase 'a community' (ummatun) as referring to a specific subset rather than the entire populace, drawing parallels to Ibrahim and the people of Musa. Furthermore, he contextualizes the 'greatest jihad' of speaking truth to a tyrannical imam as conditional upon the leader's receptiveness, highlighting the pragmatic wisdom in Shia jurisprudence regarding social stability.
